extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers, journalists, and policymakers interested in X/Twitter history, platform policy, and content moderation
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the standards, practices, and criteria X (formerly Twitter) uses or has used for account management, content moderation, transparency, and legal compliance. Covers platform actions (suspensions, removals, labels), community moderation features, and jurisdictional/ regulatory responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspension for sharing 'harmful QAnon-associated content'
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter suspended more than 70,000 accounts, stating that they shared 'harmful QAnon-associated content' at a large scale, and were 'dedicated to the propagation of this conspiracy theory across the service'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: one of the suspended accounts was then-former-president Trump's account; enforcement can include high-profile accounts and lead to litigation/settlement (Trump suit settled in 2025).

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of fake accounts used in state influence operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter identified and shut down fake accounts created by state-linked influence operations (e.g., over 7,000 Iranian-created fake accounts between January and July 2017).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These removals target coordinated inauthentic behavior attributed to states; attribution may be reported by Twitter but source identification can sometimes be uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification labels for political candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter partnered with Ballotpedia to add special labels verifying the authenticity of political candidates running for election in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to indicate account authenticity of political candidates; part of measures to combat misuse around elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement of manipulation and spam policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter removed thousands of accounts for violating manipulation policies (e.g., 5,929 accounts attributed to a Saudi state-run operation; part of a larger group reported as 88,000 engaged in spammy behavior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twitter may not disclose every related account (some could be legitimate accounts taken over through hacking). Enforcement targets coordinated manipulation, spam, and centralized behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal/suspension of coordinated influence campaigns (multi-language/targeted campaigns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter suspended accounts running campaigns to influence specific audiences (e.g., around Jamal Khashoggi assassination, Saudi accounts operating in English and Arabic that commented on U.S. media outlets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focuses on coordinated campaigns that amplify narratives across languages and target media or public opinion; platform may suspend networks even if exact source is unidentified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Displaying account transparency metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: X began displaying various information on user accounts (location, history, username changes) to combat bots and malicious accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to increase transparency and help users/media identify likely inauthentic accounts; experts noted inconsistencies and potential for 'rage farming' or foreign influence despite metadata disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and differing treatment of benign vs. malicious bots
rubrics_metrics.description: A bot is a program that can automatically tweet/retweet and follow; benign bots may generate creative content and product updates, whereas malicious bots can make unpopular people seem popular, push irrelevant products, and spread misinformation, spam or slander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform recognizes both useful and harmful bot behavior; detection/removal efforts target malicious bots that amass influence (e.g., sway elections, affect markets). Estimates of fake/bot accounts have varied widely (e.g., 20 million in 2013; 2020 estimate ~15%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing pornographic content if marked 'sensitive'
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter allows pornographic content as long as it is marked 'sensitive' by uploaders, which puts it behind an interstice and hides it from minors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This policy enabled adult content creators to market and grow businesses (e.g., link to paywalled services). Internal projects to monetize adult content faced practical/identity-verification challenges (e.g., Real ID).

rubrics_metrics.name: Age verification for access to sensitive content (jurisdictional compliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: X uses Age Verify with ID or Photo Selfie for users to access sensitive content like pornography in the UK, EU and EEA to comply with the Online Safety Act 2023 and the EU's Digital Services rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurisdiction-specific compliance mechanism intended to prevent minors from accessing sensitive content; reflects legal/regulatory obligations in certain regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community Notes / Birdwatch as community-driven moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: Birdwatch (later Community Notes) was launched as a moderation tool to debunk misinformation, with pilots and contributors proposing notes and randomized users rating them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design features included aliases to limit identity bias, expansion from pilot cohorts (1,000 → 10,000 → 15,000), and attempts to scale while ensuring usefulness; metrics (notes per day, contributor activity) used to evaluate program effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling tweets with misinformation / 'manipulated media' labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter announced policies to label tweets containing misinformation (e.g., during COVID-19) and applied 'manipulated media' labels to specific tweets (e.g., a tweet by Sambit Patra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling is a moderation tool to inform readers rather than remove content; enforcement varied over time (e.g., later changes under new ownership affected labeling practices).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with legal removal requests and government takedowns
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter received legal demands from many countries and cooperated in removing content or hiding tweets in response to government requests; transparency reports published removal counts and country sources (e.g., Turkey, Russia, France, Germany).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform balances legal compliance with transparency; large-scale takedowns have occurred during curfews or political crises (e.g., Jammu and Kashmir).

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of propaganda and state-linked misinformation accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter removed large numbers of propaganda accounts linked to governments (e.g., >175,000 accounts spreading biased narratives for Chinese Communist Party, United Russia, or Erdogan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies and removes accounts showing centralized/ coordinated behavior that push state narratives; removals have targeted multiple countries and parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition and removal of child sexual exploitation and non-consensual sexual content
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports and lawsuits allege Twitter failed to remove child sexual exploitation (CSE) and non-consensual sexual content; internal reports said Twitter could not accurately detect CSE at scale; civil suits (e.g., John Doe v. Twitter) and NCMEC filings argued Twitter did not remove illegal tweets despite notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to remove such content led to advertiser boycotts and legal exposure; platform moderation and detection technology investment (or lack thereof) is central to compliance and reputational risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation / policy changes under new ownership affecting enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Following ownership changes, Twitter eliminated the misinformation moderation team and stopped enforcing certain labeling policies; the company also pulled out of voluntary EU anti-disinformation programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational changes can materially affect how explicitly stated policies are enforced; reviewers should consider not just written policy but operational staffing and participation in external programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of AI-generated sexual/deepfake content (Grok scandal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports that X's integrated chatbot (Grok) allowed users to generate non-consensual sexualized or pornographic images, including of minors, prompting criticism, calls for bans, and legal scrutiny for facilitating sexual abuse and deepfakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points to the need for policies and technical safeguards governing AI-generated content, especially non-consensual imagery and sexual deepfakes; enforcement failures can trigger legislative and legal responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party audits and regulatory settlements regarding data privacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter agreed to pay settlements (e.g., $150 million in May 2022 to DOJ and FTC) concerning use of email addresses and phone numbers for targeted advertising and agreed to third-party audits of its data privacy program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory settlements impose ongoing compliance requirements (audits, changes to data practices) that influence platform policy and technical operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform blocking and judicial compliance in national jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: X has been banned or intermittently blocked in countries (e.g., Russia, Iran, China, North Korea) and has at times complied with or contested national orders (e.g., India ordering account blocks or Brazil blocking X for alleged non-compliance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform must navigate national laws and courts; compliance or resistance can lead to service outages, legal action, or negotiated resumptions of service.
